title: Poisoning the Well
description: To commit a preemptive *[ad hominem (abusive)](https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Ad-Hominem-Abusive)* attack against an opponent.  That is, to prime the audience with adverse information about the opponent from the start, in an attempt to make your claim more acceptable or discount the credibility of your opponent’s claim.
logical_form:
Adverse information (be it true or false) about person 1 is presented.

Therefore, the claim(s) of person 1 will be false.

examples.example: Tim: Boss, you heard my side of the story why I think Bill should be fired and not me.  Now, I am sure Bill is going to come to you with some pathetic attempt to weasel out of this lie that he has created.
examples.explanation: Tim is *poisoning the well* by priming his boss by attacking Bill’s character, and setting up any defense Bill might present as “pathetic”.  Tim is using this fallacious tactic here, but if the boss were to accept Tim’s advice about Bill, she would be committing the fallacy.

examples.example: I hope I presented my argument clearly.  Now, my opponent will attempt to refute my argument by his own fallacious, incoherent, illogical version of history.
examples.explanation: Not a very nice setup for the opponent.  As an audience member, if you allow any of this “poison” to affect how you evaluate the opponent’s argument, you are guilty of fallacious reasoning.

exceptions:
Remember that if a person states facts relevant to the argument, it is not an *[ad hominem (abusive)](https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Ad-Hominem-Abusive)* attack.  In the first example, if the other “poison” were left out, no fallacy would be committed.

Tim: Boss, you heard my side of the story why I think Bill should be fired and not me.  Now, I am sure Bill is going to come to you with his side of the story, but please keep in mind that we have two witnesses to the event who both agree that Bill was the one who told the client that she had ugly children.

**Variation:** The *appeal to ethos* involves rejection of an argument based on a character attack of the person making the argument.

*Gertie: Tony says that the movie starts at 8:00 tonight.*
*Jane: Well, Tony is misogynist pig!*
*Gertie: Hmm, we better double check that time then. *

**Fun Fact: **To understand how powerful priming the audience with adverse information can be, consider the Rosenhan experiment where eight mentally healthy students and researchers briefly feigned auditory hallucinations in order to get admitted to psychiatric hospitals. After admission, they said they were no longer having hallucinations and acted normally. One of the patients, who was also a student, was taking notes for the experiment which was interpreted as pathological “writing behavior” by one of the hospital staff.
references: Walton, D. (1998). *Ad Hominem Arguments*. University of Alabama Press.
description_et: Ennetava *[ad hominem (abusive)](https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Ad-Hominem-Abusive)* rünnaku sooritamiseks vastase vastu.  See tähendab, et anda publikule algusest peale ebasoodne teave vastase kohta, et muuta teie väide vastuvõetavamaks või vähendada vastase väite usaldusväärsust.
logical_form_et:
Esitatakse kahjulikku teavet (olgu see tõsi või vale) isiku 1 kohta.

Seetõttu on 1. isiku väide(d) vale.
exceptions_et:
Pidage meeles, et kui inimene esitab argumendiga seotud fakte, ei ole see *[ad hominem (kuritahtlik)](https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Ad-Hominem-Abusive)* rünnak.  Esimeses näites, kui teine ​​"mürk" välja jätta, ei tehtaks eksitust.

Tim: Boss, sa kuulsid minu poolt loost, miks ma arvan, et Billi tuleks vallandada ja mitte mind.  Nüüd olen kindel, et Bill tuleb teie juurde loo oma poolega, kuid pidage meeles, et meil on kaks sündmuse tunnistajat, kes mõlemad nõustuvad, et Bill oli see, kes ütles kliendile, et tal on koledad lapsed.

**Variatsioon:** *eetose poole pöördumine* hõlmab argumendi tagasilükkamist, mis põhineb argumendi esitaja iseloomurünnakul.

*Gertie: Tony ütleb, et film algab täna õhtul kell 8.00.*
*Jane: Noh, Tony on naistevihkaja siga!*
*Gertie: Hmm, me parem kontrollime seda aega siis. *

**Lõbus tõsiasi: **Selleks, et mõista, kui võimas võib olla publiku ebasoodsa teabega varjamine, kaaluge Rosenhani eksperimenti, kus kaheksa vaimselt tervet õpilast ja teadlast teesklesid psühhiaatriahaiglasse pääsemiseks korraks kuulmishallutsinatsioone. Pärast vastuvõtmist ütlesid nad, et neil ei ole enam hallutsinatsioone ja nad käitusid normaalselt. Üks patsientidest, kes oli samuti üliõpilane, tegi eksperimendi jaoks märkmeid, mida üks haiglatöötajatest tõlgendas patoloogilise "kirjutamiskäitumisena".

examples_et.example: Tim: Boss, sa kuulsid minu poolt loost, miks ma arvan, et Billi tuleks vallandada ja mitte mind.  Nüüd olen kindel, et Bill tuleb teie juurde haletsusväärse katsega sellest valest, mille ta on loonud.
examples_et.explanation: Tim *mürgitab kaevu*, rünnates oma ülemust, rünnates Billi tegelaskuju ja seades sisse kaitsemehhanismid, mida Bill võib „haletsusväärsena” esitada.  Tim kasutab siin seda ekslikku taktikat, kuid kui ülemus võtaks Timi nõuande Billi kohta vastu, teeks ta eksituse.

Tim is using this fallacious tactic here, but if the boss were to accept Tim’s advice about Bill, she would be committing the fallacy.

examples_et.example: Loodan, et esitasin oma argumendi selgelt.  Nüüd püüab mu vastane minu väidet ümber lükata oma eksliku, ebajärjekindla ja ebaloogilise ajalooversiooniga.
examples_et.explanation: Vastase jaoks pole just ilus seadistus.  Publiku liikmena, kui lasete sellel "mürgil" mõjutada seda, kuidas vastase argumente hindate, olete süüdi ekslikes arutlustes.
